info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

you must use the gather_evidence tool.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title

        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) is an additive manufacturing technology that is gaining increasing interest in aerospace, automotive and biomedical applications due to the possibility of processing lightweight alloys such as AlSi10Mg and Ti6Al4V. Both these alloys have microstructures and mechanical properties that are strictly related to the type of heat treatment applied after the L-PBF process. The present review aimed to summarize the state of the art in terms of the microstructural morphology and consequent mechanical performance of these materials after different heat treatments. While optimization of the post-process heat treatment is key to obtaining excellent mechanical properties, the first requirement is to manufacture high quality and fully dense samples. Therefore, effects induced by the L-PBF process parameters and build platform temperatures were also summarized. In addition, effects induced by stress relief, annealing, solution, artificial and direct aging, hot isostatic pressing, and mixed heat treatments were reviewed for AlSi10Mg and Ti6AlV samples, highlighting variations in microstructure and corrosion resistance and consequent fracture mechanisms.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>With the increasing industrial implementation of additively manufactured metal parts, the welding of such components gains importance. Due to size limitations of laser powder-bed fusion (PBF-LB) machines and design constraints, subsequent joining processes are required. However, the weld seam quality of PBF-LB manufactured parts, particularly aluminum parts, is still limited by pore formation in the weld seam. These pores are believed to be primarily caused by the agglomeration of hydrogen. Therefore, this study investigates the pore formation during laser beam welding of PBF-LB manufactured AlSi10Mg parts by means of in-situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging. In addition, an in-situ laser powder drying process is investigated to reduce the hydrogen content of PBF-LB manufactured aluminum parts in order to prevent the formation of hydrogen porosity during the subsequent welding process. Results show that pores predominantly form in the interdendritic region at the solidification front due to the locally increased hydrogen concentration. By applying laser powder drying, the hydrogen content can be reduced by up to 25%, thereby effectively preventing the formation of hydrogen pores.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Due to its lightweight, high strength, good machinability, and low cost, aluminum alloy has been widely used in fields such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and construction. Traditional manufacturing processes for aluminum alloys often suffer from low material utilization, complex procedures, and long manufacturing cycles. Therefore, more and more scholars are turning their attention to the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process for aluminum alloys, which has the advantages of high material utilization, good formability for complex structures, and short manufacturing cycles. However, the widespread promotion and application of LPBF aluminum alloys still face challenges. The excellent printable ability, favorable mechanical performance, and low manufacturing cost are the main factors affecting the applicability of the LPBF process for aluminum alloys. This paper reviews the research status of traditional aluminum alloy processing and LPBF aluminum alloy and makes a comparison from various aspects such as microstructures, mechanical properties, application scenarios, and manufacturing costs. At present, the LPBF manufacturing cost for aluminum alloys is 2–120 times higher than that of traditional manufacturing methods, with the discrepancy depending on the complexity of the part. Therefore, it is necessary to promote the further development and application of aluminum alloy 3D printing technology from three aspects: the development of aluminum matrix composite materials reinforced with nanoceramic particles, the development of micro-alloyed aluminum alloy powders specially designed for LPBF, and the development of new technologies and equipment to reduce the manufacturing cost of LPBF aluminum alloy.

Abstract:
Powder spattering and splashing in the melt pool are common phenomena during Laser-based Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) of metallic materials having high fluidity. For this purpose, analytical and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models have been deduced for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The single printed layer’s dimensions were estimated using primary operating conditions for the analytical model. In CFD modelling, the volume of fluid and discrete element modelling techniques were applied to illustrate the splashing and spatter phenomena, providing a novel hydrodynamics CFD model for LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The computational results were compared with the experimental analyses. A trial-and-error method was used to propose an optimized set of parameters for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. Laser scanning speed, laser spot diameter and laser power were changed. On the other hand, the powder layer thickness and hatch distance were kept constant. Following on, 20 samples were fabricated using the LPBF process. The printed samples’ microstructures were used to select optimized parameters for achieving defect-free parts. It was found that the recoil pressure, vaporization, high-speed vapor cloud, Marangoni flow, hydraulic pressure and buoyancy are all controlled by the laser-material interaction time. As the laser-AlSi10Mg material interaction period progresses, the forces presented above become dominant. Splashing occurs due to a combination of increased recoil pressure, laser-material interaction time, higher material’s fluidity, vaporization, dominancy of Marangoni flow, high-speed vapor cloud, hydraulic pressure, buoyancy, and transformation of keyhole from J-shape to reverse triangle-shape that is a tongue-like protrusion in the keyhole. In the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy, only the conduction mode melt flow has been determined. For multi-layers printing of AlSi10Mg alloy, the optimum operating conditions are laser power = 140 W, laser spot diameter = 180 µm, laser scanning speed = 0.6 m/s, powder layer thickness = 50 µm and hatch distance = 112 µm. These conditions have been identified using sample microstructures.

Abstract:
One of the most important factors during Laser Powder Bed Fusion is a robust and stable process to generate reproducibly dense and crack-free components with the same homogenous and fine-grained microstructure. Among other factors, surface tension influences the robustness of this process. Three aluminum alloys were investigated by means of 3D laser printing with respect to their ability to form lightweight and high-performance structures. The alloys include two Al-Cr based alloys (Zicromal®: Al-Cr-Zr-Mn, Scancromal®: Al-Cr-Sc-Zr) and an Al-Mg based alloy (Scalmalloy®: Al-Mg-Sc-Mn-Zr). The surface tensions of their liquid melts were measured by means of the oscillating droplet method in electromagnetic levitation. Scalmalloy® exhibited a surface tension that was by 3-8% smaller than the other two alloys, over a temperature range of 500 K above their liquidus temperature; the evaporation analysis showed that Scancromal® exhibits significantly less evaporation compared to the other two alloys by an order of magnitude. During the Laser Powder Bed Fusion process, Scalmalloy® presented the most unstable melt dynamics, and Scancromal® appeared to be more robust and stable with less weld spatters and negligible dust deposition, as evidence from the high-speed video observations. The results support the idea that surface tension and evaporation are potentially crucial factors influencing the melt dynamics and also demonstrate the capability of additive manufacturing that produces customized aluminum alloys for aerospace applications.

Al alloys processed by AM technologies are extensively investigated and play an increasing role in the production of aircraft structural parts. Based on the recent literature and research activity of the authors, this work examines advantages and drawbacks involved in the printing of Al alloys. Abstract:
The manufacturing sector is a major contributor to global energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, positioning sustainability as a critical priority. Aluminum, valued for its lightweight and recyclable properties, plays a vital role in advancing energy-efficient solutions across transportation and aerospace industries. The processing of aluminum alloys through laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), a cutting-edge additive manufacturing technology, enhances sustainability by optimizing material usage and enabling innovative lightweight designs. Based on the published literature, the present study analyzed the ecological impacts of aluminum PBF-LB/M manufacturing through life cycle assessment, circular economy principles, and eco-design strategies, identifying opportunities to reduce environmental footprints. The study also stated the critical challenges, such as the high energy demands of the aluminum PBF-LB/M process and its scalability limitations. Potential sustainable solutions were discussed starting from powder production techniques, as well as optimized processes and post-processing strategies. By adopting an interdisciplinary approach, this research highlighted the pivotal role of PBFed aluminum alloys in achieving sustainable manufacturing goals. It provided actionable insights to drive innovation and resilience in industrial applications, offering a roadmap for balancing environmental stewardship with the demands of high-performance standards.

Abstract:
The use of pure copper and Inconel 718 as cryogenic materials has been well known in the cryogenic materials space. Despite their potential, little is known about the use of these materials in cryogenic environments regarding their ability to withstand these conditions when manufactured using Additive Manufacturing (AM) methods. AM has emerged as a promising production method due to its ability to produce complex geometries and near net-shape parts. Copper and Inconel 718 offer a wide range of uses in cryogenic applications, as Copper being highly conductive makes it ideal for electrical applications, whilst Inconel 718 serves well as an engineering material. In this paper, we demonstrate the Coldgas Spraying (CS) of copper and the Selective Laser Melting (SLM) of Inconel 718 and Scalmalloy as the AM processes of choice for each respective material. The main distinction between both processes is that CS is useful for rapid deposition of material in the range of several kg/h whereas SLM is limited to a range of several hundred g/h. The work presented here was performed in the framework of a research project named AdHyBau. It is funded by the German government in which several partners from industry and academia seek to jointly develop a 500 kW output power electric drive for aviation applications which employs liquid hydrogen as a propellant for a fuel cell but also for advanced cooling to obtain very high power densities in the range of above 10 kW/kg.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the friction stir welding (FSW) of a CuNiSiCr alloy produced by laser powder bed fusion and the role of post-weld heat treatments in the microstructural evolution and mechanical performance of welded joints. The as-built alloy exhibited columnar grains, porosity, and lack-of-fusion defects. FSW refined the microstructure within the stir zone (SZ) and dramatically reduced porosity, both in pore number and size, as revealed by X-ray tomography. Mechanical testing showed that FSW joints outperformed the as-built specimens, with increased yield and tensile strengths, albeit with reduced ductility. Aging at 500 °C markedly enhanced hardness across both the base material and the SZ, achieving peak values of about 195 HV after 2 h. Peak-aged joints reached yield and tensile strengths that were 17% and 16% higher, respectively, than those of the base alloy. Direct aging proved as effective as conventional solution treatment and aging, simplifying the heat treatment route. These findings show that FSW followed by direct aging offers a promising approach for obtaining high-performance joints, providing a viable pathway for producing large, complex, additively manufactured CuNiSiCr assemblies with improved structural integrity.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The capability for synergistic advancements in both making and shaping afforded by additive manufacturing (AM) enables the flexible production of high-performance components. Boosted by the growing demand for heat-resistant aluminum alloys in the moderate-temperature weight-critical applications, AM of heat-resistant aluminum alloys constitutes a burgeoning field. Although numerous advances have emerged in recent years, there remains a gap in the review literature elucidating the newly-developed alloy systems and critically evaluating the efficacy. This state-of-the-art review presents a detailed overview of recent achievements on the heat-resistant aluminum alloy development. It begins with the introduction of various AM technologies and the pros and cons of each technique are evaluated. The enhancement mechanisms associated with printability and high-temperature properties of AM aluminum alloys are then delineated. Thereafter, the various additively manufactured aluminum alloy systems are discussed with regard to the microstructure, heat resistance and high-temperature performance. An emphasis is put on the powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB) as it has garnered significant attention for heat-resistant aluminum alloys and the vast majority of the current studies are based on this technique. Finally, perspectives are outlined to provide guidance for future research.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM)-fabricated high-strength aluminum (HS-Al) alloys (2xxx, 6xxx, and 7xxx) tend to produce fatal metallurgical defects such as porosity and cracks. Since Al is the most important lightweight structural material in automotive and aviation industries, successful printing of HS-Al alloys is in high demand. Therefore, this review focuses on the formation mechanisms and research advancements to address these metallurgical defects. Firstly, the process optimization strategies, including AM parameter optimization, hybrid AM processes, and post-processing treatment, and their effectiveness and limitations have been reviewed thoroughly. However, process optimization can address defects such as porosity, surface roughness, and residual stresses but has limited effectiveness on cracking alleviation. Secondly, the research efforts on composition modification to address cracking in AM of HS-Al alloys are critically discussed. Different from process optimization, composition modification alters the solidification dynamics in AM of HS-Al alloys and hence is considered the most promising route for crack-free printing.

Abstract:
Environmentally friendly aviation is one of the great challenges of this century. One promising approach is electric flight, in which an energy carrier (e.g. liquid Hydrogen LH2) and an electric powertrain work together. Within the scope of the joint project AdHyBau, the overarching goal is the development of new additive processes and fibre composite-metal hybrid designs for use in the cryogenic environment of such an electric propulsion system. Additive manufacturing of complex components for use in the cryogenic temperature range down to 20K (LH2) is one essential component in the production. For the design and optimization of the different components it is necessary to know the thermo-physical behaviour of such materials like high purity copper, Ti6Al4V alloy, Al-Mg-Sc alloy, and Inconell 718. The thermo-physical parameters investigated are thermal expansion, thermal & electrical conductivity and heat capacity. Further production-related influences coming from the method used (SLM, DED or Cold-Spray) and orientational dependences are discussed. Supported by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action of the Federal Republic of Germany. Grant-No.: 20M1904D.

Abstract:
Scalmalloy® is an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy designed for the additive manufacturing of components used in various industrial applications. It is primarily used in aerospace and automotive fields due to its low density and high strength. The present brief review aims to outline the state-of-the-art heat treatments currently applied on the as-built Scalmalloy®. The as-built alloy shows yield strength values of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0% due to its bimodal microstructure, which is formed by fine and coarse grain zones. These microstructural features lead to an isotropic behaviour of the mechanical properties. Varying the process parameters, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength can reach values higher than 300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively, maintaining an isotropic behaviour. After direct aging heat treatment (325 °C × 4 h), the yield and ultimate tensile strength values increase up to 456–469 MPa and 512–521 MPa, respectively, while the strain decreases to 12.0–13.0% due to phase precipitation in the α-Al matrix. Notably, the bimodal microstructure remains largely unchanged. The HIP treatment, carried out at 325 °C × 4 h with a pressure of 1000 bar, reduced the porosity (approximatively 0.18%), resulting in further improvements. The yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength rose to 482–493 MPa and 523–547 MPa, respectively.

Abstract:
Lightweight aluminum (Al) alloys have been widely used in frontier fields like aerospace and automotive industries, which attracts great interest in additive manufacturing (AM) to process high-value Al parts. As a mainstream AM technique, laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) shows good scalability to meet the requirements for large-format component manufacturing and repair. However, LDED Al alloys are highly challenging due to their inherent poor printability (e.g. low laser absorption, high oxidation sensitivity and cracking tendency). To further promote the development of LDED high-performance Al alloys, this review offers a deep understanding of the challenges and strategies to improve printability in LDED Al alloys. The porosity, cracking, distortion, inclusions, element evaporation and resultant inferior mechanical properties (worse than laser powder bed fusion) are the key challenges in LDED Al alloys. Processing parameter optimizations, in-situ alloy design, reinforcing particle addition and field assistance are the efficient approaches to improving the printability and performance of LDED Al alloys. The underlying correlations between processes, alloy innovation, characteristic microstructures, and achievable performances in LDED Al alloys are discussed. The benchmark mechanical properties and primary strengthening mechanism of LDED Al alloys are summarized. This review aims to provide a critical and in-depth evaluation of current progress in LDED Al alloys. Future opportunities and perspectives in LDED high-performance Al alloys are also outlined.

Abstract:
This study aims to explore the effect of microstructural parameters on the notch fatigue damage behavior of the TC21 alloy. Different levels of lamellar microstructures were achieved through distinct aging temperatures of 550 °C, 600 °C, and 650 °C. The findings reveal that increasing aging temperature primarily contributes to the augmentation of α colony (αc) thickness, grain boundaries α phase (GBα) thickness, and α fine (αfine) size alongside a reduction in α lath (αlath) thickness and αfine content. The notch alters stress distribution and relaxation effects at the root, enhancing notched tensile strength while weakening plasticity. Moreover, the increased thickness of GBα emerges as a critical factor leading to the increase area of intergranular cleavage fracture. It is noteworthy that more thickness αlath and smaller αfine facilitate deformation coordination and enhance dislocation accumulation at the interface, leading to a higher propensity for micro-voids and micro-cracks to propagate along the interface. Conversely, at elevated aging temperatures, thinner αlath and larger αfine are more susceptible to fracture, resulting in the liberation of dislocations at the interface. The reduction in αlath thickness is crucial for triggering the initiation of multi-system dislocations at the interface, which promotes the development of persistent slip bands (PSBs) and dislocation nets within αlath. This phenomenon induces inhomogeneous plastic deformation and localized hardening, fostering the formation of micro-voids and micro-cracks.

Abstract:
Research on powder-based additive manufacturing of aluminium alloys is rapidly increasing, and recent breakthroughs in printing of defect-free parts promise substantial movement beyond traditional Al–Si–Mg) systems. One potential technological advantage of aluminium additive manufacturing, however, has received little attention: the design of alloys for use at T > ∼200°C, or ∼1/2 of the absolute melting temperature of aluminium. Besides offering lightweighting and improved energy efficiency through replacement of ferrous, titanium, and nickel-based alloys at 200–450°C, development of such alloys will reduce economic roadblocks for widespread implementation of aluminium additive manufacturing. We herein review the existing additive manufacturing literature for three categories of potential high-temperature alloys, discuss strategies for optimizing microstructures for elevated-temperature performance, and highlight gaps in current research. Although extensive microstructural characterisation has been performed on these alloys, we conclude that evaluations of their high-temperature mechanical properties and corrosion responses are severely deficient.

Abstract:
This paper first examines crack growth in a range of tests on additively manufactured (AM) and conventionally manufactured Inconel 718. It is shown that whereas when the crack growth rate (da/dN) is plotted as a function of the range of the stress intensity factor (ΔK), the crack growth curves exhibit considerable scatter/variability, when da/dN is expressed in terms of the Schwalbe crack driving force (Δκ), then each of the 33 different curves essentially collapse onto a single curve. This relationship appears to hold over approximately six orders of magnitude in da/dN. The same phenomenon also appears to hold for 20 room temperature tests on both conventionally and additively manufactured Inconel 625. Given that the 53 studies examined in this paper were taken from a wide cross section of research studies it would appear that the variability in the da/dN and ΔK curves can (to a first approximation) be accounted for by allowing for the variability in the fatigue threshold and the cyclic fracture toughness terms in the Schwalbe crack driving force. Abstract:
Stainless-steel is extensively utilized in the key structural components of the main equipment in the nuclear island of pressurized water reactor nuclear power plants. The operational experience of nuclear power plants demonstrates that stress corrosion is one of the significant factors influencing the long-term safe operation of stainless steel in the high-temperature water of pressurized water reactor nuclear power plants. This study is based on the stress corrosion crack growth rate data of 316SS and 304SS stainless steel in the simulated primary water environment of pressurized water reactor nuclear power plants. Data mining and modeling were conducted using multiple machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and the Sharpley Additive explanation (SHAP) method was employed to analyze the interpretability of the model. The results indicate that the stress corrosion crack growth rate prediction model based on XGBoost outperforms other models in all assessment indicators. Compared with empirical equations, XGBoost exhibits high flexibility and excellent data-driven learning capabilities. In the test set, 90% of the prediction errors are within the range of experimental values, with the maximum error multiple being 2.5, which significantly improves the prediction accuracy. Moreover, the distribution of SHAP values is consistent with the theoretical study of the stress corrosion behavior of stainless-steel, effectively reflecting the impact of cold working, temperature, and stress intensity factor on the stress corrosion crack growth rate, thereby proving the reliability of the model’s prediction results. The achievements of this study hold significant reference value and application prospects for the prediction of the stress corrosion behavior of stainless-steel in a high-temperature and high-pressure water environment of pressurized water reactor nuclear power plants.

Abstract:
Recent studies have proposed a simple formula, which is based on Elber’s original approach to account for R-ratio effects, for determining the crack closure-free ΔKeff versus da/dN curve from the measured R-ratio-dependent ΔK versus da/dN curves. This approach, which is termed “Simple Scaling,” has been shown to collapse the various R-ratio-dependent curves onto a single curve. Indeed, this approach has been verified for a number of tests on metals, polymers, and a medium-entropy alloy. However, it has not yet been used to help assess/determine the closure-free ΔKeff versus da/dN curve. The current paper addresses this shortcoming and illustrates how to use this methodology to assess the ΔKeff versus da/dN curves given in the open literature for tests on a number of steels, aluminum alloys, STOA Ti-6Al-4V, a magnesium alloy, and Rene 95. As such, it would appear to be a useful tool for assessing fatigue crack growth.

Abstract:
Aluminum (Al) and its alloys are the second most used materials spanning industrial applications in automotive, aircraft and aerospace industries. To comply with the industrial demand for high-performance aluminum alloys with superb mechanical properties, one promising approach is reinforcement with ceramic particulates. Laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF) of Al alloy powders provides vast freedom in design and allows fabrication of aluminum matrix composites with significant grain refinement and textureless microstructure. This review paper evaluates the trends in in situ and ex situ reinforcement of aluminum alloys by ceramic particulates, while analyzing their effect on the material properties and process parameters. The current research efforts are mainly directed toward additives for grain refinement to improve the mechanical performance of the printed parts. Reinforcing additives has been demonstrated as a promising perspective for the industrialization of Al-based composites produced via laser powder-bed fusion technique. In this review, attention is mainly paid to borides (TiB2, LaB6, CaB6), carbides (TiC, SiC), nitrides (TiN, Si3N4, BN, AlN), hybrid additives and their effect on the densification, grain refinement and mechanical behavior of the LPBF-produced composites.

                                    Chair: Jacob Leachman


     To leverage the increasingly rare resources that are available through aerospace, ease of

air and space access must be improved. Although the cost of these aerospace missions has been

reduced by up to three orders of magnitude, the millions of dollars that are required to access

space limit the rate by which these resources can be utilized. Therefore, alternative methods to

reduce the cost of air and space flight must be explored. Some of these methods include the

reduction of vehicle mass and improved part efficiency and performance. The additive

manufacturing (AM) of polymer matrix composites (PMCs) presents a unique option for

reducing the mass of aerospace vehicles and thereby the cost required for launch. Also, there are

many AM metal matrix composite (MMC) systems that can increase part efficiency and

performance. These solutions also have the potential to reduce the cost of terrestrial applications

where cryogenic temperatures are present. Thus, this thesis explores the mechanical

characterization of these materials at cryogenic temperatures and the effect material deviations

have on part mass and performance. To assert accurate data obtainment in all material




                                                 ivcharacterization, the mechanical load frame utilized for mechanical data acquisition, the

Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester (CRAFT), is first detailed herein. Next, a mechanical

characterization of the additively manufactured AlSi10Mg alloy and an MMC alternative are

obtained. Third, the mechanical performance of an additively manufactured PMC liquid

hydrogen tank constituent is collected in addition to an analysis on the effect the processing

parameters have on the mechanical behavior. These developments permitted the

recommendation for alternative material and processing parameter selections that have the

potential to reduce launch vehicle dry mass and improve application performance. Beyond the

observed improvements detailed within this thesis, the data acquired encourages further

cryogenic design optimization through modifications made to material selection and

development.

   At room temperature, specimens survived 107 cycles at 30% and 50% of room temperature

UTS (41.75 MPa). At 20 K, the specimens survived 107 cycles at 50% of 20K UTS (54.33 MPa)

(Hunt, 2021). Although a data point for 30% UTS at 20 K was not obtained, the lack of part failure

at 50% UTS would suggest that 30% may be well below the material fatigue limit. Unfortunately,

assessment of result accuracy would have been insufficient due to lack of cryogenic fatigue

property data of PMC materials in literature and no samples failing during testing. However, future

work will focus on collecting more fatigue data points for result validation. Furthermore, collecting

sufficient fatigue test data points at higher loads and varying frequencies will allow for developing

an S-N curve for the nylon-11 PMC. Doing so will aid in modifying the nylon-11 PMC based on

loads and frequencies forecasted for specific cryogenic applications.



2.5 CONCLUSIONS

   The systems and capabilities of the novel Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester were

demonstrated. CRAFT utilizes various systems to perform mechanical testing on most material

classes in a liquefied hydrogen environment. CRAFT can test at temperatures as low as 14 K and

a frequency up to 100 Hz. Moreover, static and dynamic forces of 8.5kN and 12 kN, respectively




                                      20are attainable. These capabilities allow tests to simulate the cryogenic environment and loading

scenarios characteristic of cryogenic applications.

   Preliminary data were obtained and analyzed to assess the validity of CRAFT data acquisition.

A glass microbead and carbon fiber reinforced nylon-11 material was tensile and tension-tension

fatigue tested. At 20 K, the PMC maintained an ultimate tensile strength 30% greater when

compared to the room temperature tensile strength. The elastic modulus at 20 K was 24% lower

than room temperature. Uncharacteristically, tensile properties at 20 K were less than they were at

77 K; at 77 K, elastic modulus was 253% greater than the room temperature value. Lastly, there

was a decrease in elongation at break between room temperature and 20K of 84% while the

elongation at break increased by 100% between room temperature and 77K. It is proposed that

future work should be performed to characterize and identify the source of this phenomenon.

Fatigue testing was performed at 30% or 50% of the UTS at room temperature or 20 K. No samples

failed in the allowed 107 cycles. Therefore, future research should be conducted at greater force

amplitudes and frequencies to obtain a characteristic S-N curve.

   By detailing CRAFT systems and introductory findings, CRAFT can now be utilized for

future materials research on the nylon-11 PMC and other additively manufactured materials.

Obtaining a complex understanding of AM PMC cryogenic mechanical performance ensures

safe material selection and design for cryogenic applications. This also offers the opportunity for

future optimization of 3D-printed PMCs.

AlSi10Mg alloy is commonly used in additive manufacturing as this material possesses a high

mechanical strength and corrosion resistance (and easy to process via Laser-based AM). Also,

AlSi10Mg has the potential to be implemented in aerospace applications due to a low density.

With cryogenic environments being characteristic of many aerospace applications, it is essential

to identify the performance of this aluminum alloy at cryogenic temperatures. However, there

currently exists a lack of material data on the AlSi10Mg alloy at 20 Kelvin. Consequently, any

modeling of this material would be inaccurate and inconsistent at cryogenic temperatures.

AlSi10Mg can be more accurately modeled and optimized for cryogenic environments seen in

aerospace applications with more accurate data. Thi

AlSi10Mg can be more accurately modeled and optimized for cryogenic environments seen in

aerospace applications with more accurate data. This study developed mechanical analysis of

A6061-T651, AlSi10Mg, and A6061-RAM2 at 20K. A6061-T651 was chosen to validate data

acquisition of the Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester (CRAFT). The A6061-RAM2 was

selected as a possible alternative to AlSi10Mg as the A6061 matrix of this material has a greater

thermal conductivity at room temperature and a potentially improved mechanical performance

due to the ceramic additive. XY and Z print directions of all materials were mechanically tested,

analyzed, and compared. As a result, a full characterization of the three materials was obtained.

An assertion of the material with the greatest mechanical performance was made.

       Other literature has suggested that there are materials alternative to the AlSi10Mg that

may be better suited for cryogenic environments that demand high thermal conductivities. More

specifically, additives have the potential to improve the mechanical performance of the matrix

they are added to. Li presents a study where selective laser melted (SLM) AlSi10Mg tensile

properties are compared to those with an additional 1.0% by weight TiB2 (Li, 2020). The




                                      22addition of 1.0 weight percent ceramic resulted in the increase of ultimate tensile strength (UTS),

yield strength (YS), and elongation by 9.73%, 64.4%, and 4.57% over the base alloy,

respectively (Li, 2020). The addition of the load-bearing ceramic improved the tensile strength,

which presents a possible increase over AlSi10Mg. Also, the thermal conductivity of 6061-T651

aluminum is greater than AlSi10Mg at room temperature. At room temperature, the thermal

conductivity of 6061-T651 is 167 W/m-K, whereas additively manufactured AlSi10Mg is 103 ±

5 W/m-K and 119 ± 5 W/m-K for the XY and Z print orientations, respectively (Kaiser

Aluminum), (EOS Aluminum). Therefore, a 6061 aluminum that features ceramic reinforcement

has the potential to increase the mechanical strength as well as the thermal conductivity if

employed in cryogenic applications. Moreover, the matrix of this metal matrix composite

(MMC) would maintain identical CTE properties to the 6061-aluminum spacer plates it would be

mounted to. Therefore, A6061-RAM2 from Elementum 3D was selected as a material to

compare with that of the AlSi10Mg tensile data at 20K. Improved tensile performance would

promote A6061-RAM2 usage over AlSi10Mg in cryogenic applications.



3.2 MATERIALS AND METHODS

3.2.1 Materials

Materials tested are A6061-T651, A6061-RAM2, and AlSi10Mg. The latter two materials were

produced via selective laser melting (SLM) in an EOS M290 printer whereas the A6061-T651

was produced through traditional manufacturing methods. The A6061-T651, an aged and

solution heat treated aluminum alloy, was chosen to prove the validity of data obtained for the

system at room and cryogenic temperatures. The A6061-T651 aluminum composition by weight

percent was 0.40-0.80% silicon, up to 0.7% iron, 0.15-0.40% copper, up to 0.15% manganese,




                                      230.8-1.2% magnesium, 0.04-0.35% chromium, up to 0.25% zinc, up to 0.15% titanium, up to

0.15% other elements, and aluminum as the remainder (Kaiser Aluminum). The mechanical

performance of AlSi10Mg was developed through testing performed at 20K. The A6061-RAM2

was selected as an alternative to this AlSi10Mg. The reason is that A6061-RAM2 has high

ultimate tensile and yield strengths and faster build speed. The chemical composition of these

additively manufactured metals was not made available. Visser Precision manufactured the

AlSi10Mg tensile specimens, Elementum 3D manufactured the A6061-RAM2 tensile specimens,

and Kaiser Aluminum manufactured the 6061-T651. The AlSi10Mg was originally selected

because it has high strengths, adequate thermal conductivity, and accessibility for additive

manufacturing. The additively manufactured materials, AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2 did not

T651 was tested at room temperature to compare to the material data sheets provided by the

material supplier (Kaiser Aluminum). This material was also tested at 20K to compare with what

allowed for a direct comparison in mechanical performance at 20K and promoted the use of

A6061-RAM2 over AlSi10Mg in cryogenic applications.

                                      263.3 THEORY/CALCULATION

3.3.1 Mechanical Performance of Additively Manufactured Aluminum Alloys at Cryogenic

Temperatures

Additive manufactured materials maintain a certain degree of anisotropy. This is due to the

directionality of how the part is printed. Additively manufactured materials will exhibit the

greatest tensile performance when loaded in the direction parallel with the print direction. This is

because samples loaded normal to the print direction rely more on the interlayer adhesion

strength than the bulk material’s mechanical performance. For this experiment, data were

obtained for both directions to compare how the different print directions impacted ultimate

tensile strength and elastic modulus data.

      There currently exists a lack of material data at cryogenic temperatures. No material data

was found for the AlSi10Mg at cryogenic temperatures, but for the A6061-RAM2, it maintains a

tensile strength of 419 ± 11 MPa and a yield strength of 378 ± 11 MPa near 116 K (Elementum

A6061-RAM2). There is no mention of corresponding print orientation. These strengths at 116 K

showed an increase of 24.0% for the ultimate tensile strength and 21.5% for the yield strength

compared to room temperature data. This data from Elementum 3D shows a continual increase

of ultimate tensile strength, yield strengths, and elongation as the temperature decreases from

room temperature.

     One study looked at a medium entropy alloy, CrCoNi, and how respective mechanical

properties differed between 293 K, 195 K, and 77K. Samples were additively manufactured

using selective laser melting (SLM) and maintained a particle size distribution of 15 to 53 µm

(Han, 2021). Exhibited in this research was an increase in yield, ultimate tensile strengths, and

elongation as temperature decreased. Between room temperature and 77K, the yield strength




                                      27increased by 32.1%, and the UTS increased by 43.9%. Overall, the strength and elongation

values increased at cryogenic temperatures due to an increase in the number of dislocations at 77

K (Han, 2021).

      Another study examined the effect of cryogenic temperatures on FeCoNiCr alloy

mechanical performance (Bae, 2018). All samples were produced through the employment of

vacuum induction melting equipment. A visually apparent difference exists between 298K and

77K in ultimate tensile strength and Young’s modulus. Due to cryogenic embrittlement, the UTS

and modulus both increase at 77K when compared to the stress-strain data obtained at room

temperature.

      Zhang identified a similar relationship with mechanical testing of a titanium alloy at

room temperature, 200K and 77K. The samples here are composed of TiNb36Ta2Zr3O0.35 and

were produced by cold isostatic pressing and vacuum sintering; these samples were then heat-

treated at 1273K for 1 hour in argon (Zhang, 2019). Again, between room temperature and 77K,

we see an observed rise in ultimate tensile strength, Young’s Modulus, and strain at break.

        Lastly, this trend in the increased mechanical performance of metallic alloys at cryogenic

temperatures was captured by Dong. A stress-strain curve of an Al0.06CoCrFeNi2Mo0.08V0.04 alloy

at room temperature and approximately 203K and 77K was produced in this report (Dong, 2021).

Although there is no apparent increase in elastic modulus between room temperature and 77K,

there is an obvious increase in UTS once again. This trend seems to be universally applicable to

most metallics and is expected to hold true in the testing of all three metallics tested in this

report. Strain at break seemed to be maximum for the material when tested at -70°C, and

Young’s modulus was greatest at room temperature.





                                      283.3.2 Mechanical Performance of Ceramic-Reinforced Metal Matrix Composites

One study conducted by Ezatpour et al. reinforced Al6061 using nano-Al2O3 particles and

studied how the strength of this material was impacted. The non-reinforced as-cast Al6061 had a

yield strength of 85 MPa and tensile strength of 110 MPa. After being reinforced with .5 wt%

Al2O3, the yield and tensile strength increased to 175 MPa and 215 MPa, an increase of 105.9%

and 95.5%, respectively (Ezatpour, 2014). This trend continued to increase both yield and

ultimate tensile strengths. However, adding 1.5% showed a decrease in mechanical properties

from the addition of 1.0%. Here the yield strength decreased from 250 MPa to 200 MPa, and the

UTS decreased from 260 MPa to 210 MPa for the as-cast state, suggesting a peak performance to

nano-particle reinforcement ratio (Ezatpour, 2014). For the A6061-RAM2 tested in this

experiment, a 2% ceramic additive was added. Due to the dramatic improvement of using the

Al2O3 ceramic additive in A6061, it is expected that the ceramic in the A6061-RAM2 should

also show improvement in yield and tensile strengths.

3.5.1 Mechanical Findings

The ultimate tensile strength and Young’s modulus data increased for all materials between room

temperature and 20K except the Young’s modulus of the AlSi10Mg in the Z print direction.




                                      34Also, the mechanical performance of the A6061-RAM2 was better than the AlSi10Mg aluminum

alloy at 20K. This is demonstrated by an improved ultimate tensile strength and Young’s

modulus in both print orientations at this 20K testing temperature. The anisotropy of AM seems

to be less present with the selective laser melted materials. This is observed by the different print

orientations maintaining similar mechanical performances. This is most likely due to the melting

of powder in the SLM process. Melting of this powder is better for resultant adhesion between

print layers compared to the solid-state diffusion of SLS. It is recommended that alternative

additives and respective contents be explored more in depth for thermal and mechanical

improvement capabilities at 20K. Different additives and additive contents may improve the

mechanical and thermal performance of the A6061 material beyond what was demonstrated in

the findings of this report.

3.5.2 Error Considerations

Upon finalizing data acquisition, a source of error was identified and included herein. The cross-

sectional areas input in the MTS Testsuite software were measured at room temperature. Because

of the samples’ experience between room temperature and 20K, the resultant ultimate tensile

strength provided will be less than the actual. Although there is no known coefficient of thermal

expansion data available for the AlSi10Mg materials tested at 20K, 6061-T651 aluminum is

approximated to have a linear expansion of -4.15E-3 m/m at 20K (Veres). This linear expansion

can approximate the reduction in cross-sectional areas of the 6061 aluminum and 6061 matrix

aluminum, A6061-RAM2. Based on this linear expansion data, the cross-sectional area of these

6061 aluminum-based samples would reduce the cross-sectional area by 0.8% between room

temperature and 20K. This would result in an increase of the reported ultimate tensile strength of

these materials of 0.8%. Another error identified was with the recorded ultimate tensile strengths

                                      37         CHAPTER FOUR: POLYMER MATRIX COMPOSITE TESTING

4.1 INTRODUCTION

4.1.1 Background

The additive manufacturing (AM) of polymer matrix composites (PMCs) presents a unique

opportunity for liquid cryogen fuel storage due to a shortened development lifecycle, reduced

cost, and high specific strength. Additive manufacturing can reduce the time between initial

concept and part implementation. Moreover, AM offers reduced costs for complex or low print

quantity parts compared to traditional manufacturing methods. PMCs offer a unique trait in

achieving the structural performance of metallics at a reduced mass. Greater than 60% of launch

vehicle dry mass is attributed to the fuel and cryogenic tank (Li, 2022). Because this mass makes

up a majority of launch vehicle dry mass, higher specific strength alternative tank constituents,

have been proposed. Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) cryogenic fuel tanks can offer

mass savings between 20-40% by weight compared to aluminum alternatives (Li, 2022). This

can reduce the mass required to store these liquid cryogens, doing the same for the vehicle they

are employed in.

    Metallics have been the status quo for cryogenic fuel storage due to withstanding extreme

thermomechanical cycles. However, at the Hydrogen Properties for Energy Research (HYPER)

Laboratory, a selective laser sintered (SLS) PMC cryogenic fuel tank has been developed. This

tank is composed of the EOS material PA840-GSL, a carbon fiber and glass microbead

reinforced polyamide 11 material. The tank comprises five PMC shells with alternating layers of

aerogel insulation and vapor ducts (Adam, 2017). Figure 4.1 is a cross-section of the tank design.





                                      38       Figure 4.1 Additively Manufactured Liquid Hydrogen Fuel Tank Cross-Section.

   The tank constituent is over-engineered for the mechanical requirements of the application it

is employed in. The lowest burst pressure testing results have been at approximately 150 psig

compared to the 25 psig required for normal operation. Similarly, the first (hoop) and second

(axial) principal stresses for the tank have been modeled to be 43 MPa and 40 MPa, respectively;

the hoop stress maintains a 2.2 factor of safety and the axial stress a 1.8 factor of safety (Adam,

2017). Initial tensile testing of the constituent material has shown an ultimate tensile strength

over two times the 43 MPa hoop stress and almost two times the 40 MPa axial stress. Given that

this tank is in early development, the material performance mechanically exceeds what is

prescribed for application, and there are thermal property benefits that come from the reduction

of mechanical performance. The work herein focuses on improving tank thermal insulation by

reducing the mechanical strength of the constituent closer to what is required for operation. This

is done by manipulating selected print parameters of the tank material.

4.1.2   Selective Laser Sintering

Selective laser sintering is an AM method where fine material particles are fused together by a

pulsed CO2 laser (Bandyopadhyay, 2016). The build plate translates along the Z-axis with each

sintered layer, and additional powder is evenly distributed above the previous layer. This process

continues until the input 3D CAD model is complete. SLS features a variety of process




                                      39parameters that determine resultant part properties such as performance, tolerance, and surface

finish. Four parameters of interest are the hatch spacing, layer height, laser speed, and laser

power. Manipulation of these parameters has changed part density which impacts many of the

resulting part performance metrics. Although research has been done to identify the impact of

layer height, laser speed, and laser power on printed part performance, minimal research exists

on hatch spacing manipulation (Ho, 1999) (Tomanek, 2021) (Tong, 2020) (Czelusniak, 2020)

(Kim, 2021). Therefore, hatch spacing, which can be varied until un-sintered particles with low

thermal conductance contact points exist between fused layers, was the parameter investigated in

this study.

polyamide 11. Samples were selective laser sintered by Northwest Rapid Manufacturing in an

thermomechanical performance. To determine the range of parameters to be used for the design

paths, the energy density in which the material melts and the energy density used for normal

not made available, 0.290 J/mm3 was identified as the energy of melt for a similar EOS

4.3 THEORY/CALCULATION

4.3.1 Energy Density Manipulation

The four parameters outlined in the introduction, laser power, laser speed, hatch spacing, and

layer thickness, are all related by energy density. This energy density parameter is formulaically

defined below.

                    𝐸=

Where P is the laser power (W), v is the laser speed (mm/s), h is the hatch spacing (mm), and t is

the layer thickness (mm). Energy density holds significance on the final part porosity and



                                      42thereby density. The relationship between supplied energy density, part density, and resultant

tensile strength have been explored in many publications. For example, Ho looks at the effect

that energy density has on the density and mechanical performance of DTM Laserite

Polycarbonate Compound LPC-3000. In this study, laser power varied between 11 and 31 watts

to achieve variation in supplied energy density (Ho, 1999). As energy density is increased, part

density and tensile strength both increase as well. However, as the energy density increases

further, the density and tensile strength begin to decrease. This phenomenon is dependent upon

the energy of melt and energy of degradation of the polycarbonate being studied. Exceeding the

energy of melt results in increased part density up to a maximum. Thereafter, as the energy of

degradation is approached, the density and thereby the tensile strength taper off. The maximum

density and tensile strength were identified as being 1056 kg/mm3 and 34 N/mm2 respectively.

The maximum density occurs at a supplied energy density of 0.09 J/mm2 whereas the maximum

tensile strength occurred closer to 0.10 J/mm2 (Ho, 1999). It is visually apparent that the

correlation between the energy density and the tensile strength is significant. Another takeaway

lies in the difference in tensile performance when the part is printed normal to or parallel with

the loading axis. Parts printed parallel with the loading axis have a notable mechanical

improvement over the samples printed normal to the loading axis. The relationship between

energy density and part density can be expanded a step further when considering the effect on

thermal conductivity.

   This consideration is explored by Tomanek in an article where the thermal performance of

selective laser melted (SLM) 304L stainless steel in a fully dense form is compared to an

attempted 3%-part porosity form (Tomanek, 2021). The porosity was achieved through

increasing the hatch spacing and scan speed of the SLM process. The fully dense parts were




                                      43printed with an energy density of 58.8 J/mm3 while the nominal 3% porosity parts maintained an

energy density of 38.1 J/mm3 (Tomanek, 2021). Tomanek’s data shows that the porous X-print

orientation parts maintained a 5.4% reduction in density and a 9.9% reduction in thermal

conductivity when compared to the fully dense X-print orientation parts. Similarly, the porous Y-

print orientation parts had a density and thermal conductivity 0.9% and 3.2% less than the fully

dense alternatives, respectively (Tomanek, 2021). By reducing the energy density below

maximized energy density, it can be expected that the resultant part density will be reduced. This

will cause a subsequent reduction in tensile strength and thermal conductivity as previously

hypothesized.

  An additional study looking into the effect that laser energy density has on the mechanical

performance of a printed part was researched by Tong (Tong, 2020). This publication looks at

the tensile strength of thermoplastic phenolic resin-coated ceramic at a variety of laser energy

densities and laser spot sizes. Laser power was set to either 100 or 450 watts whereas scan

spacing ranged between 0.05 mm to 2.20 mm to achieve laser energy densities ranging from

0.067 J/mm2 to 0.667 J/mm2 (Tong, 2020). Again, a maximized tensile strength is observed at a

laser energy density between the material energy of melt and energy of degradation for both a

0.6 mm and 3.0 mm laser spot diameter. The maximized tensile strength for a 0.6 mm laser spot

diameter print was observed at a laser energy density of 0.133 J/mm2 whereas the maximum

tensile strength of a 3.0 mm laser spot diameter print was identified at a laser energy density of

0.150 J/mm2 (Tong, 2020).

energy density of a carbon-fiber reinforced PA12 from EOS. SLS energy density was varied to

obtain tensile strength, elastic modulus, strain, and part density. To achieve the energy density




                                      44range of 0.096 J/mm3 to 0.493 J/mm3, laser power ranged from 30 to 45 W, laser scan speed

varied from 2000 to 5000 mm/s, and scan spacing ranged from 0.2 to 0.6 mm. All parts were

printed in the X-orientation. The maximum average density was found to 1.03 g/cm3 at the

plateau around 0.181 J/mm3. The highest elastic modulus and tensile strength values were 3669

MPa and 65 MPa respectively (Czelusniak, 2020). Like the previously presented data, all

mechanical data and the part density follow the trend of increased performance up to a maximum

value and deterioration thereafter. In addition, there is a visual correlation between part density

and the resultant mechanical performance of the parts tested.

desirable thermal properties may be enhanced. It has been shown in literature that the increase of

scan spacing has resulted in improved thermal insulation. One study in particular looks at the

effect that the hatch spacing and scan speed parameters have directly on the thermal conductivity

of the resultant print. The material being tested was an AlSi10Mg alloy printed via SLM. The

laser power for these samples was maintained at 285 W and the scan speed and hatch spacing for

the standard printing case were 1700 mm/s and 0.12 mm, respectively. The scan spacing for the

other print configurations were either 1530 mm/s or 1870 mm/s whereas the hatch spacing for

these alternative configurations was eight 0.10 mm or 0.14 mm. This resulted in energy densities

ranging from 39.93 J/mm3 to 55.88 J/mm3 (Kim, 2021). As shown above, there is a notable

decrease in the thermal conductivity of AlSi10Mg as the scan speed and hatch spacing are

increased. Moreover, the thermal conductivity is greatest for the polar angle of 90 degrees. 45-

degree and 0-degree orientations both see continual reductions in thermal conductivity of the

AlSi10Mg material.

                Abstract. The use of pure copper and Inconel 718 as cryogenic materials has been well known
                  in the cryogenic materials space. Despite their potential, little is known about the use of these
                  materials in cryogenic environments regarding their ability to withstand these conditions when
                manufactured using Additive Manufacturing (AM) methods. AM has emerged as a promising
                 production method due to its ability to produce complex geometries and near net-shape parts.
               Copper and Inconel 718 offer a wide range of uses in cryogenic applications, as Copper being
                 highly conductive makes it ideal for electrical applications, whilst Inconel 718 serves well as an
                 engineering material.

                 In this paper, we demonstrate the Coldgas Spraying (CS) of copper and the Selective Laser
                Melting (SLM) of Inconel 718 and Scalmalloy as the AM processes of choice for each respective
                  material. The main distinction between both processes is that CS is useful for rapid deposition
                 of material in the range of several kg/h whereas SLM is limited to a range of several hundred
                   g/h. However, CS can only yield bulk structures while SLM allows the production of fine and
                    intricate structures due to the nature of their approaches.

              The work presented here was performed in the framework of a research project named AdHyBau.
                       It is funded by the German government in which several partners from industry and academia
                seek to jointly develop a 500 kW output power electric drive for aviation applications which
               employs liquid hydrogen as a propellant for a fuel cell but also for advanced cooling to obtain
                very high power densities in the range of above 10 kW/kg.


1. Introduction and motivation
Several partners from industry and academia cooperate in a funded research project named AdHyBau
to develop an electric drive and its required subsystems, all running on liquid hydrogen to allow for
green aerial transportation with zero carbon emissions. The focus of the authors lies on the development
of the electric drive train along with investigating Additive Manufacturing (AM) processes to enable
new designs and new production methods for optimization of an innovative electric drive. Its design and
scope of use is aimed towards replacing turbine engines in e.g. small commuter aircrafts, also known as
turboprop engines.
  Among the most important goals of the project are those directly linked to the drive design. One of
them is an efficient coil design and optimized cooling systems through AM for a high power density of
at least 10 kW/kg. Another goal is to employ cryogenic hydrogen as a cooling medium on one hand and
as an energy source on the other hand. Also, lightweight design and hybrid structures with fiber-
reinforced composites and additively manufactured metal components are intended to be incorporated
to optimize overall results.

2. State-of-the-art

2.1. Cryogenic Materials
In the realm of cryogenic materials, recent advancements in metallic materials used in engineering
applications, particularly for the design of electric drives operating at extremely low temperatures were
achieved. Remarkable properties of certain metallic materials when exposed to cryogenic conditions at
and below 77 K were identified. For instance, specific high-strength alloys, like titanium alloys and
nickel-based superalloys but also aluminum and aluminum alloys, have demonstrated exceptional
mechanical resilience and improved thermal conductivity at cryogenic temperatures, making them ideal
candidates for electric drive components subjected to extreme cold environments [5].
   The ongoing developments in cryogenic engineering have led to the emergence of innovative
electrically conductive and non-conductive materials for efficient cooling and enabled the utilization of
these  metallic  materials  to enhance  the performance and  efficiency  of  electric  drives. These
advancements hold immense potential to revolutionize the design and application of electric propulsion
systems, offering significant benefits in line with the goals of the project presented here.

2.2. Additive Manufacturing (AM)
Little is known about the properties of AM materials in cryogenic applications, however, the high degree
of freedom for geometrical design allowed by AM should encourage further exploration into this space
beyond the current state-of-the-art designs, as new cryogenic component designs are developed.
Conventional manufacturing processes employ subtractive technologies such as milling, turning, sawing
and drilling and create components by taking material away. AM processes, however, build up material
in layers from scratch. Their underlying principle typically comprises the application of a material in a

In the case of solid materials these can be employed in the form of powder, wire or sheets as shown in
