Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We present the COSMOS Spectroscopic Redshift Compilation encompassing ∼20 yr of spectroscopic redshifts within a 10 deg
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    area centered on the 2 deg
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    COSMOS legacy field. This compilation contains 487,666 redshifts of 266,284 unique objects from 138 individual programs up to
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     ∼ 8 with median stellar mass ∼10
                    <jats:sup>8.4</jats:sup>
                    –10
                    <jats:sup>10</jats:sup>
                    <jats:italic>M</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>⊙</jats:sub>
                    (redshift dependent). Rest-frame
                    <jats:italic>NUVrJ</jats:italic>
                    colors and star formation rate–stellar mass correlations show that the compilation primarily contains low-to-intermediate-mass star-forming and massive, quiescent galaxies at
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     < 1.25 and mostly low-mass bursty star-forming galaxies at
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     > 2. Sources in the compilation cover a diverse range of environments, including protoclusters such as “Hyperion.” The full compilation is 50% spectroscopically complete by
                    <jats:italic>i</jats:italic>
                     ∼ 23.4 mag and
                    <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>s</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                     ∼ 21.6 mag; however, this is redshift dependent. Spatially, the compilation is >50% (>30%) complete within the central (outer) region limited to
                    <jats:italic>i</jats:italic>
                     < 24 mag and
                    <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>
                      <jats:italic>s</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sub>
                     < 22.5 mag, separately. We demonstrate how the compilation can be used to validate photometric redshifts and investigate calibration metrics. By training self-organizing maps on COSMOS2020/Classic and projecting the compilation onto it, we find key subpopulations currently lacking spectroscopic coverage, including
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     < 1 intermediate-mass quiescent and low-/intermediate-mass bursty star-forming galaxies,
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     ∼ 2 massive quiescent galaxies, and
                    <jats:italic>z</jats:italic>
                     > 3 massive star-forming galaxies. The ability to design and produce compliant mechanisms
by Additive Manufacturing (AM) was investigated in
several projects. In the last ten years, significant progress
were made  especially on  design  and  optimization
software as well as on the possibility of printing thin
metallic structures. Nevertheless, compliant mechanisms
are pushing AM and current process simulation solutions
to their limits, presenting significant challenges to fully
benefit from this new process [1].
Four  projects  were  completed  at CSEM  with  the
development,  production  and  testing  of  compliant
mechanisms made by AM. The advantages proposed by
AM were confirmed, such as the possibility to design and
produce very complex shapes and the ability to combine
various functions. Printing monolithic structures with
flexible  areas  linked by  rigid elements,  fast design

{"answer": "## Answer

**Yes—tensile properties have been measured at liquid-hydrogen temperature, not just at 77 K.** Adams, Rinauro and Leachman reported direct **20 K tensile tests in liquid hydrogen** on selective-laser-melted AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2 (DOI: **10.1088/1757-899X/1302/1/012006**). The underlying Washington State University thesis identifies an EOS M290 as the machine used to make both aluminum materials; it is therefore an LPBF/SLM study. Five specimens of each alloy were tested in each of two build orientations. The thesis is dated May 2022 on its title page, although its repository record is indexed as 2023; the 2024 paper reports the same results rather than a second independent campaign. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021)

The measured 20 K ultimate tensile strengths (UTS) and elastic moduli are summarized below; the uncertainties are **standard errors**, not standard deviations. The authors state that the specimens equilibrated overnight at 20 K before testing. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000030)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**What remains unverified at approximately 4 K:** I did not find a published, specimen-level **4–4.2 K tensile, fracture-toughness or fatigue result** for an LPBF aluminum alloy, nor a verified **20 K fracture-toughness or fatigue result**. This is a limit of the located literature, not proof that no laboratory has performed such tests. Despite its name, the *Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester* was used for **tensile** testing of the aluminum specimens in the Adams study; the paper reports UTS and modulus, not aluminum fatigue life or fracture toughness. It also reports no aluminum elongation because the strain-gauge range was exceeded. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022)

Several close-looking reports do not establish the requested properties at 20 or 4 K:

- **Scalmalloy:** Rehme and Weidermann describe SLM Scalmalloy specimens and say initial cryogenic tests gave unsatisfactory results, leading them to drop planned additional tensile and low-cycle-fatigue specimens. They provide neither the Scalmalloy test temperature nor quantitative mechanical results, so the report cannot establish a 20 K or 4 K property. Weiss and colleagues measured SLM Scalmalloy **thermophysical** properties down to about 4 K—including conductivity, thermal expansion and heat capacity—not the requested mechanical properties. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040)
- **A205/A20X-family alloy:** Tumulu reports LPBF A205 tensile and instrumented Charpy-impact measurements at **−196 °C (approximately 77 K)**. Charpy absorbed energy is not a standard fracture-toughness value, and these tests are not at 20 or 4 K. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000042)

**Bottom line:** the answer is **yes for LPBF aluminum tensile strength and modulus at 20 K**, with directly reported data for **AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2**. A measured LPBF-aluminum **4 K tensile property**, or **20/4 K fracture-toughness or fatigue property**, was not substantiated by the sources located. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000030)"}

state.question: Has anyone measured tensile, fracture-toughness or fatigue properties of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / selective laser melting) aluminum alloys, such as AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, A20X or other AM aluminum alloys, at liquid-hydrogen (about 20 K) or liquid-helium (about 4 K) temperature, rather than only at 77 K?

answer.question: Has anyone measured tensile, fracture-toughness or fatigue properties of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / selective laser melting) aluminum alloys, such as AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, A20X or other AM aluminum alloys, at liquid-hydrogen (about 20 K) or liquid-helium (about 4 K) temperature, rather than only at 77 K?
answer.answer:
Yes. ## Answer

**Yes—tensile properties have been measured at liquid-hydrogen temperature, not just at 77 K.** Adams, Rinauro and Leachman reported direct **20 K tensile tests in liquid hydrogen** on selective-laser-melted AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2 (DOI: **10.1088/1757-899X/1302/1/012006**). The underlying Washington State University thesis identifies an EOS M290 as the machine used to make both aluminum materials; it is therefore an LPBF/SLM study. Five specimens of each alloy were tested in each of two build orientations. The thesis is dated May 2022 on its title page, although its repository record is indexed as 2023; the 2024 paper reports the same results rather than a second independent campaign. (adams2023materialandscan pages 1-8, adams2023materialandscan pages 33-37, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 1-3, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5)

The measured 20 K ultimate tensile strengths (UTS) and elastic moduli are summarized below; the uncertainties are **standard errors**, not standard deviations. The authors state that the specimens equilibrated overnight at 20 K before testing. (adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 5-8, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths media b6484a21)

| SLM/LPBF alloy | Orientation | Mean UTS (MPa) ± SE | Mean Young’s modulus (GPa) ± SE | *n* |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| AlSi10Mg | XY | 483 ± 21 | 73.5 ± 4.70 | 5 |
| AlSi10Mg | ZX | 512 ± 43 | 65.1 ± 3.30 | 5 |
| A6061-RAM2 | XY | 568 ± 16 | 76.1 ± 0.65 | 5 |

contexts.context: The Tumulu 2025 excerpt provides direct evidence of mechanical testing of laser powder bed fused A205 aluminum-copper metal matrix composite below 77 K. Tensile tests were conducted at -196 °C and room temperature for both as-built (AB) and heat-treated (HT) conditions. Tensile strength was comparable at the two temperatures, while low temperature eliminated serrations in the AB stress-strain response and increased elongation for the HT condition; AB and HT reportedly had comparable elongation to fracture. The excerpt also reports Charpy impact testing at -196 °C, which is a dynamic fracture/impact test rather than a conventional fracture-toughness test. Crack propagation was easier at low temperature in both conditions. Crack-initiation energy was unchanged from room temperature for AB material but increased for HT material. The fracture mode changed with heat treatment: AB samples showed transgranular fracture, whereas HT samples showed intergranular fracture. The passage does not report a conventional fracture-toughness measurement (such as K_IC or J_IC), fatigue testing, or thermal-property-only measurements. Thus, for the requested comparison, Tumulu 2025 is clear evidence of sub-77 K tensile and Charpy testing for A205, but it does not establish sub-77 K fatigue or standard fracture-toughness data.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide the exact measured 20 K tensile-strength and modulus results for AlSi10Mg or A6061-RAM2; the A6061 results table and subsequent discussion appear to be outside the supplied pages. Testing used the CRAFT apparatus at HYPER, with liquid hydrogen maintained at 2.7 bar, vacuum of 1E-5 mBar, and overnight equilibration at 20 K. Both materials were manufactured by selective laser melting in an EOS M290 printer and tested in XY and Z orientations, with five tensile specimens per material/orientation condition. Testing followed ASTM D638 using type V specimens in a cryogenic test system (CRAFT). The study calculated ultimate tensile strength and Young’s modulus from measured stress–strain data; it also used low-temperature strain gauges and thermal-strain compensation. A6061-T651 was included as a conventionally manufactured validation material and was tested at room temperature and 20 K, while the two additively manufactured materials were tested at 20 K. The excerpt does not provide numerical tensile results, fatigue data, or fracture-toughness data, and it contains no tests at 4 K or 4.2 K. contexts.context: The excerpt documents Adams, Rinauro, and Leachman (2024) as a direct experimental cryogenic tensile study conducted at 20 K, using ASTM D638 specimens and the CRAFT apparatus in liquid hydrogen. The study included conventionally manufactured A6061-T651 for validation and additively manufactured materials, with print orientation investigated for the anisotropic specimens. Samples were thermally equilibrated overnight at 20 K, and ultimate tensile strength and elastic modulus were measured; elongation was not reported because the strain-gauge limit was exceeded. For A6061-T651, the excerpt reports a literature 20 K UTS of 497 ± 8 MPa and Young’s modulus of 77.8 ± 0.7 GPa, while the article’s experimental comparison is used to validate the test system. However, this excerpt does not provide direct 4 K/4.2 K data, fatigue data, or fracture-toughness data, nor does it establish any additional study beyond Adams et al. 2024 for LPBF AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, A205/A20X, or A6061-RAM2. Fatigue testing was conducted at **room temperature**, yielding an infinite-life bending stress of **230 MPa** and **450 MPa at 10⁴ cycles**. Thus, it provides no evidence of AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, A20X, or other LPBF aluminum property measurements at 20 or 4 K.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone measured tensile, fracture-toughness or fatigue properties of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF / selective laser melting) aluminum alloys, such as AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, A20X or other AM aluminum alloys, at liquid-hydrogen (about 20 K) or liquid-helium (about 4 K) temperature, rather than only at 77 K?

Yes. ## Answer

**Yes—tensile properties have been measured at liquid-hydrogen temperature, not just at 77 K.** Adams, Rinauro and Leachman reported direct **20 K tensile tests in liquid hydrogen** on selective-laser-melted AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2 (DOI: **10.1088/1757-899X/1302/1/012006**). The underlying Washington State University thesis identifies an EOS M290 as the machine used to make both aluminum materials; it is therefore an LPBF/SLM study. Five specimens of each alloy were tested in each of two build orientations. The thesis is dated May 2022 on its title page, although its repository record is indexed as 2023; the 2024 paper reports the same results rather than a second independent campaign. (adams2023materialandscan pages 1-8, adams2023materialandscan pages 33-37, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 1-3, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5)

The measured 20 K ultimate tensile strengths (UTS) and elastic moduli are summarized below; the uncertainties are **standard errors**, not standard deviations. The authors state that the specimens equilibrated overnight at 20 K before testing. (adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 5-8, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths media b6484a21)

| SLM/LPBF alloy | Orientation | Mean UTS (MPa) ± SE | Mean Young’s modulus (GPa) ± SE | *n* |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| AlSi10Mg | XY | 483 ± 21 | 73.5 ± 4.70 | 5 |
| AlSi10Mg | ZX | 512 ± 43 | 65.1 ± 3.30 | 5 |
| A6061-RAM2 | XY | 568 ± 16 | 76.1 ± 0.65 | 5 |
| A6061-RAM2 | ZX | 516 ± 41 | 77.8 ± 2.76 | 5 |
| **Test/source** | **Liquid hydrogen, 20 K** | **Direct tensile testing** | **Adams et al. (2024), Table 4** | **(adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 5-8, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths media b6484a21)** |


*Table: Direct liquid-hydrogen tensile results from Adams, Rinauro, and Leachman (2024), Table 4, DOI 10.1088/1757-899X/1302/1/012006. These are tensile-strength and elastic-modulus measurements—not fatigue or fracture-toughness tests.*

**What remains unverified at approximately 4 K:** I did not find a published, specimen-level **4–4.2 K tensile, fracture-toughness or fatigue result** for an LPBF aluminum alloy, nor a verified **20 K fracture-toughness or fatigue result**. This is a limit of the located literature, not proof that no laboratory has performed such tests. Despite its name, the *Cryogenic Accelerated Fatigue Tester* was used for **tensile** testing of the aluminum specimens in the Adams study; the paper reports UTS and modulus, not aluminum fatigue life or fracture toughness. It also reports no aluminum elongation because the strain-gauge range was exceeded. (adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 5-8)

Several close-looking reports do not establish the requested properties at 20 or 4 K:

- **Scalmalloy:** Rehme and Weidermann describe SLM Scalmalloy specimens and say initial cryogenic tests gave unsatisfactory results, leading them to drop planned additional tensile and low-cycle-fatigue specimens. They provide neither the Scalmalloy test temperature nor quantitative mechanical results, so the report cannot establish a 20 K or 4 K property. Weiss and colleagues measured SLM Scalmalloy **thermophysical** properties down to about 4 K—including conductivity, thermal expansion and heat capacity—not the requested mechanical properties. (rehme2024additivemanufacturingof pages 1-3, rehme2024additivemanufacturingof pages 6-9, rehme2024additivemanufacturingof pages 9-9, weiss2024cryogenicthermophysicalproperties pages 6-9, weiss2024cryogenicthermophysicalproperties pages 9-11)
- **A205/A20X-family alloy:** Tumulu reports LPBF A205 tensile and instrumented Charpy-impact measurements at **−196 °C (approximately 77 K)**. Charpy absorbed energy is not a standard fracture-toughness value, and these tests are not at 20 or 4 K. (tumulu2025laserpowderbed pages 166-169, tumulu2025laserpowderbed pages 158-162)

**Bottom line:** the answer is **yes for LPBF aluminum tensile strength and modulus at 20 K**, with directly reported data for **AlSi10Mg and A6061-RAM2**. A measured LPBF-aluminum **4 K tensile property**, or **20/4 K fracture-toughness or fatigue property**, was not substantiated by the sources located. (adams2023materialandscan pages 33-37, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 3-5, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths pages 5-8, adams2024ultimatetensilestrengths media b6484a21)
